tagline: Rice fields, crawfish ponds and wetland habitat along Louisiana’s prairie roads
intro: The Flyway Byway passes rice fields and crawfish ponds in southwest Louisiana’s prairie region. It is a Louisiana Scenic Byway linking several state highways, with a branch to Lacassine National Wildlife Refuge. The Louisiana Office of Tourism promotes its agricultural landscape and birdlife, reporting more than 160 bird species along the route. The office describes a 55-mile byway and allows half a day to a day for a self-guided tour. Lake Arthur’s park and boardwalk and Lacassine National Wildlife Refuge are among its named attractions.

Travel here once followed waterways: Acadian French and African-American residents used them for transport before the railroad. At Welsh, rail service followed stagecoach traffic: Henry Welsh donated a right-of-way in 1880, and the railroad built a station. At Jennings, the Southern Pacific depot became the center of new development. Seaman A. Knapp was brought in during 1885 to demonstrate the region’s suitability for rice production.

From Jennings, follow the US 90 leg to Welsh, then LA 99 toward the country west of Lake Arthur. The LA 3056 branch reaches Lacassine National Wildlife Refuge. Continue on LA 14 to Lake Arthur, on the north shore of a tidal section of the Mermentau River. LA 26 leads north to Jennings to complete the town-to-town circuit.
notice: Rice fields and crawfish ponds are visible from the road.

moments.title: Jennings
moments.text: The railroad depot became the center of Jennings’ early growth, and settlers came from Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and other Midwestern states. Sylvester L. Cary arrived from Iowa in 1883 and wrote to friends there, encouraging them to follow. Another part of the town’s early development survives in its library. The Jennings Ladies’ Library Association opened a public library in 1889; after its first building burned in 1901, the association sought Carnegie funding. The replacement, built in 1908, has a domed octagonal entrance at the corner of its V-shaped plan. Buff brick and white woodwork distinguish the replacement library building.

moments.title: Welsh
moments.text: Henry Welsh’s cabin and store served travelers on the main stagecoach route across southern Louisiana. The stop lay between New Iberia and Texas, on land that had belonged to his father, Miles Welsh. In 1880 Henry donated a right-of-way to the Louisiana Western Rail Road, which built a station. The town was laid out that same year and incorporated in 1888, with Henry as its first mayor. The byway now connects Welsh to Jennings along US 90 and to the country west of Lake Arthur along LA 99. The Louisiana Western later became part of Southern Pacific.

moments.title: Lacassine National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Lacassine’s marshes are both natural and managed: the refuge includes 16,500 acres of freshwater marsh and open water, alongside the 16,000-acre managed Lacassine Pool. Established in 1937 for migratory birds and other wildlife, the refuge provides winter habitat for several hundred thousand ducks and geese. Managers adjust water levels to support marsh plants and plant crops to feed waterfowl using the Mississippi and Central Flyways. Wood ducks, whistling ducks and mottled ducks nest here during the breeding season. Other habitats include flooded gum and cypress trees and restored tallgrass prairie, extending the refuge’s variety beyond the open marsh.

moments.title: Lake Arthur
moments.text: Lake Arthur occupies the north shore of its namesake lake, a tidal section of the Mermentau River. Acadian families settled in the area during the late 1700s. One was Arthur LeBlanc; travelers began calling the water le lac d’Arthur, the name that evolved into Lake Arthur. Rice production gained a mill in 1876 and an irrigation pumping plant on Bayou Lacassine in 1890. The town’s park and boardwalk are among the byway’s waterfront attractions. The lake connects with the Mermentau River’s waterway to the Gulf of Mexico; boat captains were important to the lives of early settlers.
